purpose: The review criteria for this exercise were written by the project authors; they judge whether the wording is complete and workable, not legal validity.

I1.name: Unclear scope of deliverables
I1.principle: Specify the number of pages, formats, a list of source files and the delivery channel, instead of only saying the client must be satisfied.

I2.name: Unclear payment terms and costs
I2.principle: State the event that triggers payment, the deadline, invoicing, and how additional costs are approved.

I3.name: Schedule not linked to changes
I3.principle: Set delivery dates and a change-approval process; added scope should confirm both the fee and the schedule.

I4.name: No limits on acceptance and rework
I4.principle: Specify acceptance criteria, the feedback deadline, the number of revision rounds, and how out-of-scope revisions are handled.

I5.name: New work mixed up with existing materials
I5.principle: Separate new work from this project, the Designer's existing templates and third-party materials, and list what is delivered or licensed; do not assume the Designer can transfer third-party rights.

I6.name: Incomplete settlement and handover on termination
I6.principle: Agree on termination notice, payment for completed work, how refunds are calculated, and a delivery list, leaving no handover unresolved.

I7.name: No limits on use of customer data
I7.principle: Limit the purpose of use, who may access it and any public display, and agree on safekeeping, return or deletion, and obligations after termination.

source.usage: Used only as a reference for contract drafting elements such as scope of services, payment and intellectual property; Australian law is not applied to this fictional case.

boundary: Do not invent laws or case law, and do not assert that anything is certainly void or certainly wins; numbers in suggestions must be marked as options for the parties to negotiate, not as existing terms.
